summaries.summary: Large Language Models trained on webscale text have recently demonstrated unprecedented abilities across NLP tasks, using prompt inputs to guide their behavior.
The proposed algorithm assumes access to an initial prompt and i.i.d. training data consisting of input-output text pairs.
Gradient descent in this context refers to evaluating a prompt on a batch of data and creating a local loss signal that indicates how to improve the current prompt.
The gradient descent steps are used to guide a beam search over the space of prompts, which serves as the outer loop of the prompt training algorithm.
The expansion step generates many new candidate prompts from a current prompt, leveraging the conceptual gradient descent framework.
Algorithm 2 samples a minibatch from training data, evaluates the prompt on it, and collects errors.
The selection step chooses the b most promising candidates to continue on the beam for the next iteration after expansion generates successor candidates.
The algorithm samples from training data and selects prompts using UCB-based bandit strategies, updating counts and value estimates after each observation.
A preliminary case study demonstrates ProTeGi across 4 benchmark NLP tasks, finding it can exceed state-of-the-art prompt learning baselines.
While ProTeGi could be applied to various problems, the experiments focus on four NLP benchmark classification tasks.
For each task, 50 examples are sampled for development and 150 for test, with results averaged over 3 trials and reported as test set binary F1 scores.
ProTeGi is compared against nonparametric baselines that are directly comparable to the proposed framework.
ProTeGi outperforms other state-of-the-art algorithms on all four datasets, with an average improvement over the baselines.
An ablation replaces the beam search step with a single flat enumerate-then-select step to assess the benefit of beam search.
Different approximate selection algorithms from the bandit framework are experimented with to gauge their relative performance.
Related work draws from research on LLM prompts, with most prior efforts focusing on differentiable tuning of soft prompts.
The conclusion introduces Prompt Optimization with Textual Gradients (ProTeGi), a simple and general-purpose framework for automatically optimizing LLM prompts.
The limitations section acknowledges that ProTeGi's efficiency is constrained in practice by rate limiting on the LLM API, reducing effective throughput.
Figure 2 illustrates the text dialogue tree used to mimic gradient descent and overcome the discrete optimization barrier, where a feedback prompt Δ generates the gradient g from the starting prompt.
Algorithm 1 outlines the ProTeGi procedure, taking an initial prompt, beam width, search depth, and metric function as inputs and iteratively selecting prompts via beam search guided by the metric.
Table 2 compares approximate best arm identification algorithms, showing that all evaluated methods outperform uniform sampling across Jailbreak and Liar tasks at varying prompt budgets.
Table 4 presents gradient examples across models (GPT-3, InstructGPT, ChatGPT, GPT-4) for Ethos, Sarcasm, and Jailbreak tasks, with more examples referenced in the Appendix.
